u:core-oop-34-parking-lot.title: Parking Lot (LLD)
u:core-oop-34-parking-lot.summary: Model spots, vehicles, tickets and pricing — the classic object-modelling interview.

blocks.text: A parking-lot design tests clean object modelling. Start from requirements: multiple levels, spot sizes (small/medium/large), vehicles, ticketing, and fee calculation.
Core classes

items: **ParkingLot** → has many **ParkingFloor** → each has many **ParkingSpot** (with a size).
**Vehicle** (abstract) → **Car / Bike / Truck**, each mapping to compatible spot sizes.
**Ticket** — issued on entry (spot, entry time); **ParkingLot.park(vehicle)** finds a free compatible spot.
**FeeStrategy** (interface) — hourly/flat/day pricing, chosen via the **Strategy** pattern.
**EntryGate / ExitGate** issue and close tickets.

blocks.text: Design decisions to voice: use an interface for the pricing (Strategy) so rules can change; keep spot-finding behind the lot so allocation policy can evolve; make Vehicle abstract for polymorphic spot compatibility.
Concurrency matters at scale: two cars must not get the same spot. Mention a lock or atomic allocation on spot assignment.

mcqs.q: Which pattern best fits configurable parking fee rules?
mcqs.explain: Different pricing schemes are interchangeable algorithms — a natural Strategy, so rules can change without editing the lot.

mcqs.q: Making Vehicle an abstract base with Car/Bike/Truck subclasses supports:
mcqs.explain: Polymorphism lets spot allocation treat vehicles uniformly while respecting each type's size needs.

mcqs.q: A concurrency concern in a parking lot is:
options: Two vehicles being assigned the same spot without synchronization
mcqs.explain: Spot allocation is shared state; without locking/atomic assignment two vehicles could get one spot.

u:core-oop-35-url-shortener.title: URL Shortener (LLD)
u:core-oop-35-url-shortener.summary: Map long URLs to short codes and back, with collision-free code generation.

blocks.text: At the class level, a URL shortener needs to generate a unique short code, store the mapping, and resolve it back.

items: **UrlService** with `shorten(longUrl)` and `expand(code)`.
**Code generation**: base62 encode an auto-increment id (short, collision-free), or a hash + collision check.
**Repository** interface storing code → longUrl (in-memory map for LLD; a KV store at scale).
Optional: custom aliases, expiry, click counts.

blocks.text: The key LLD decision is code generation. Base62 of a unique counter guarantees uniqueness with no collision checks and yields short codes (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion). Random/hash needs collision handling.
Base62 uses [0-9a-zA-Z]; 7 characters give ~3.5 trillion combinations — plenty. This overlaps with the HLD version (see [[study-content-system]] SD pack) which adds scaling, caching, and DB choice.

mcqs.q: Base62-encoding a unique auto-increment id for the short code guarantees:
options: Uniqueness with no collision checks needed
mcqs.explain: A monotonically increasing id is unique, so its base62 encoding is unique without collision handling.

mcqs.q: Compared with hashing the URL, using a counter avoids:
mcqs.explain: Hash-based codes can collide and need checks/retries; a unique counter never collides.

mcqs.q: The core operations of the service are:
mcqs.explain: It maps a long URL to a code and resolves a code back to the long URL.

u:core-oop-36-splitwise.title: Splitwise (LLD)
u:core-oop-36-splitwise.summary: Track who owes whom across group expenses with multiple split types.

blocks.text: Splitwise records expenses and computes balances between users, supporting equal, exact, and percentage splits.

items: **User**, **Group**, **Expense** (payer, amount, participants, split).
**Split** (abstract) → **EqualSplit / ExactSplit / PercentSplit** — a **Strategy/polymorphic** hierarchy validating the split sums to the total.
**BalanceSheet** — a map of (userA → userB → amount owed); each expense updates balances.
**Simplify debts** — optionally net out cycles so fewer transactions settle the group.

blocks.text: Two design points to raise: model split types polymorphically (validate each sums correctly), and keep balances as a net directed graph so 'who owes whom' is O(1) to read and can be simplified.
Debt simplification is a graph problem: minimise transactions by netting each person's total owed vs owing.

mcqs.q: Equal, exact, and percentage splits are best modelled as:
mcqs.explain: Each split type is an interchangeable algorithm validating totals — a polymorphic Strategy design.

mcqs.q: Balances between users are conveniently stored as:
options: A map of (userA, userB) → amount owed
mcqs.explain: A directed balance map lets you read and update who owes whom efficiently.

mcqs.q: Every split type must be validated so that:
options: The parts sum to the total expense amount
mcqs.explain: Whatever the split type, the shares must add up to the full expense, or balances become inconsistent.

u:core-oop-37-elevator-system.title: Elevator system (LLD)
u:core-oop-37-elevator-system.summary: Model cars, requests, and a dispatcher that decides which elevator serves which call.

blocks.text: An elevator design tests state machines and request scheduling.

items: **Elevator** with state: current floor, **direction** (up/down/idle), a set of target floors, doors state.
**Request** — a hall call (floor + direction) or a car call (destination floor).
**Dispatcher / Controller** — assigns each hall call to the best elevator (nearest moving in the same direction).
The elevator serves floors in its current direction first (like the SCAN disk algorithm), then reverses.

blocks.text: The scheduling insight: an elevator behaves like the SCAN (elevator) algorithm — continue in one direction serving requests, then reverse. The dispatcher chooses the elevator that minimises wait, favouring same-direction proximity.
Model the elevator as a state machine (Idle → MovingUp/MovingDown → DoorsOpen). Use the State pattern if behaviour varies a lot per state.

mcqs.q: An elevator serving requests in its current direction before reversing mirrors which algorithm?
mcqs.explain: Continuing one way then reversing is exactly the SCAN/elevator approach — minimising direction changes.

mcqs.q: The dispatcher's job is to:
options: Assign each hall call to the most suitable elevator
mcqs.explain: It selects which elevator serves a call, typically the nearest one moving in the same direction.

mcqs.q: An elevator's behaviour is well modelled as a:
options: State machine (idle, moving up/down, doors open)
mcqs.explain: Clear states and transitions make a state machine (optionally the State pattern) the natural model.

u:core-oop-38-rate-limiter.title: Rate limiter (LLD)
u:core-oop-38-rate-limiter.summary: Cap how many actions a client may perform per time window — token bucket and friends.

blocks.text: A rate limiter decides whether to allow or reject a request based on a client's recent request rate. Several algorithms exist; know their trade-offs.

rows: Tokens refill at a rate; each request spends one
Allows bursts up to bucket size; most popular
Requests drain at a fixed rate (a queue)

items: **RateLimiter** interface with `allow(clientId)`; a **strategy** per algorithm.
Per-client state (tokens/counters) in a map (in-memory for LLD; Redis at scale).

blocks.text: Token bucket is the go-to answer: refill tokens at a steady rate, allow a request if a token is available. It permits controlled bursts (up to bucket capacity) while enforcing an average rate — flexible and simple.
Fixed window has a boundary problem: a burst at the end of one window and start of the next can allow 2× the limit briefly. Sliding window fixes this.

mcqs.q: The token bucket algorithm allows bursts because:
options: Accumulated tokens (up to capacity) can be spent quickly
mcqs.explain: Unused tokens accumulate up to the bucket size, so a burst can spend them, while refill enforces the average rate.

mcqs.q: The fixed-window counter's weakness is:
options: Bursts across the window boundary can allow up to 2x the limit
mcqs.explain: Requests clustered at the end of one window and start of the next both count in separate windows, briefly doubling throughput.

mcqs.q: Leaky bucket differs from token bucket by:
options: Draining requests at a fixed rate, smoothing output (no bursts)
mcqs.explain: Leaky bucket processes at a constant rate like a queue draining, smoothing traffic rather than permitting bursts.

u:core-oop-39-design-an-lru-cache-class.title: Design an LRU cache class
u:core-oop-39-design-an-lru-cache-class.summary: O(1) get/put with eviction of the least-recently-used entry — hashmap + doubly linked list.

blocks.text: An **LRU (Least Recently Used) cache** evicts the entry unused for the longest time when it's full. The interview goal is **O(1)** for both `get` and `put`.
The data structures

items: A **hash map**: key → node, for O(1) lookup.
A **doubly linked list** ordered by recency: most-recently-used at the front, least at the back.
**get(key)**: look up the node, move it to the front, return its value.
**put(key, val)**: insert/update at the front; if over capacity, remove the back node (LRU) and its map entry.

blocks.text: The combination is the whole trick: the hash map gives O(1) access; the doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering and eviction (removing a node needs both neighbours, hence *doubly* linked). Neither alone achieves O(1) for both operations.
In Java, `LinkedHashMap` with accessOrder=true implements LRU out of the box — mention it, then show you can build it from scratch.

mcqs.q: An O(1) LRU cache combines:
options: A hash map and a doubly linked list
mcqs.explain: The map gives O(1) lookup; the doubly linked list gives O(1) recency reordering and eviction.

mcqs.q: Why a DOUBLY linked list rather than singly?
options: O(1) node removal needs access to the previous node too
mcqs.explain: Removing/moving a node in O(1) requires updating both neighbours, which needs prev pointers.

mcqs.q: On a cache miss when full, put() evicts:
mcqs.explain: The tail of the recency list is the least-recently-used entry, which is evicted to make room.

u:core-oop-40-tic-tac-toe-snake-and-ladd.title: Tic-tac-toe / Snake and Ladder (LLD)
u:core-oop-40-tic-tac-toe-snake-and-ladd.summary: Model a board game: board, players, turn loop, and win/end conditions.

blocks.text: Board-game designs test clean separation of board state, players, and game rules.

items: **Board** (grid or cells), **Player**, **Game** controller running the turn loop.
Tic-tac-toe: check win after each move (rows, columns, diagonals); detect draw when the board is full.
Snake & Ladder: a **Dice**, cells with snakes/ladders (a map position → jumpTo), a queue of players; move and apply jumps until someone reaches the last cell.
Keep rule-checking (win/jump) separate from board storage and I/O.

blocks.text: The reusable lesson: separate the game LOOP (whose turn, roll/move, check end) from the RULES (win condition, snakes/ladders) and the STATE (board). This makes new games or rule changes localised.
Snakes and ladders are just a `Map<int,int>` from a cell to its destination — model both uniformly rather than as separate classes.

mcqs.q: In Snake & Ladder, snakes and ladders are cleanly modelled as:
options: A map from a cell position to its destination cell
mcqs.explain: Both simply move a player from one cell to another, so a position→destination map handles them uniformly.

mcqs.q: Good board-game design separates:
options: The game loop, the rules, and the board state
mcqs.explain: Separating loop, rules, and state keeps each concern independently changeable and testable.

mcqs.q: In tic-tac-toe, a win check is performed:
options: After each move, across rows, columns, and diagonals
mcqs.explain: Each move can complete a line, so win conditions are evaluated after every move.

u:core-oop-41-bookmyshow-seat-booking.title: BookMyShow seat booking (LLD)
u:core-oop-41-bookmyshow-seat-booking.summary: Reserve seats for a show without double-booking under concurrency.

blocks.text: The heart of a ticket-booking design is preventing two users from booking the same seat at once.

items: **Movie**, **Show** (movie + screen + time), **Screen** with **Seats**, **Booking**.
**Seat states**: available → **locked** (held during checkout) → booked. A lock has a short timeout.
**BookingService.book(show, seats, user)**: atomically lock the requested seats, take payment, then confirm; release the lock on timeout or failure.
Concurrency: use per-seat locks / a DB transaction / optimistic version so only one booking wins.

blocks.text: The critical design point is the seat's temporary LOCKED state plus an atomic lock acquisition. Without it, two concurrent users both see a seat 'available' and double-book. A timeout frees seats if the user abandons checkout.
Locking must be atomic across the whole selected set (all-or-nothing), or a user can partially book seats and block others.

mcqs.q: The key to preventing double-booking a seat is:
options: An atomic transition to a temporary LOCKED state during checkout
mcqs.explain: Atomically locking a seat while a user checks out ensures only one booking can proceed for it.

mcqs.q: A held (locked) seat should have:
options: A timeout that releases it if checkout isn't completed
mcqs.explain: A lock timeout frees abandoned seats so they don't stay unavailable indefinitely.

mcqs.q: Locking a multi-seat selection should be:
options: Atomic / all-or-nothing for the whole set
Done seat by seat with gaps
mcqs.explain: All-or-nothing locking avoids partial bookings that strand seats and confuse other users.

u:core-oop-42-load-balancing.title: Load balancing
u:core-oop-42-load-balancing.summary: Distribute traffic across servers for scale and availability, using an allocation algorithm.

blocks.text: A **load balancer** spreads incoming requests across multiple backend servers so no single one is overwhelmed, improving **throughput** and **availability** (it routes around failed servers via health checks).

rows: Send to the server with fewest active connections
Bigger servers get proportionally more traffic

blocks.text: Load balancing gives horizontal scale + high availability. Layer 4 (transport) balances by IP/port; Layer 7 (application) can route by URL/headers. Health checks let it stop sending traffic to dead servers.
For session stickiness (a user must hit the same server), use IP hash or consistent hashing — but stateless servers avoid needing stickiness at all.

mcqs.q: A load balancer improves availability by:
options: Routing traffic away from failed servers via health checks
mcqs.explain: Health checks let it stop routing to unhealthy servers, so failures don't take down the service.

mcqs.q: The 'least connections' algorithm sends a request to the server with:
mcqs.explain: It balances by current load, favouring the least busy server.

mcqs.q: Layer 7 load balancing can route based on:
options: Application data like URL path and HTTP headers
mcqs.explain: L7 (application layer) sees HTTP details, enabling content-based routing, unlike L4 which sees only transport info.

u:core-oop-43-caching-layers-and-invalid.title: Caching layers and invalidation
u:core-oop-43-caching-layers-and-invalid.summary: Store hot data closer/faster to cut latency and load — and the hard part is keeping it fresh.

blocks.text: **Caching** keeps frequently accessed data in fast storage (memory, CDN) to reduce latency and backend load. Caches appear at many layers: browser, CDN, application (Redis/Memcached), and database.
Write strategies

rows: App checks cache; on miss, loads from DB and populates cache
Writes go to cache and DB together (consistent, slower writes)
Writes go to cache, flushed to DB later (fast, risk of loss)

blocks.text: The famous hard problem: **cache invalidation** — keeping cached data consistent with the source. Use TTL expiry, explicit invalidation on writes, or write-through. Stale cache is a top source of subtle bugs.
Guard against a 'thundering herd' / cache stampede: when a hot key expires, many requests hit the DB at once. Mitigate with locks, staggered TTLs, or serving stale-while-revalidate.

mcqs.q: In the cache-aside pattern, on a cache miss the application:
options: Loads from the database and populates the cache
mcqs.explain: Cache-aside (lazy loading) fetches from the source on a miss and stores it for next time.

mcqs.q: Write-through caching trades:
mcqs.explain: Writing to both cache and DB together keeps them consistent but makes writes slower.

mcqs.q: Cache invalidation is hard because:
options: Keeping cached copies consistent with the changing source is tricky and causes stale-data bugs
mcqs.explain: Deciding when/how to refresh or evict cached entries so they match the source is a notoriously subtle problem.

u:core-oop-44-horizontal-vs-vertical-sca.title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
u:core-oop-44-horizontal-vs-vertical-sca.summary: Add more machines, or make one machine bigger — different limits and failure modes.

blocks.text: Two ways to handle more load.

Vertical scaling is simplest but hits a hardware ceiling and keeps a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling is how large systems grow — it's effectively unlimited and fault-tolerant, but requires load balancing and handling distributed state.
Horizontal scaling is far easier when servers are **stateless** (session/state kept in a shared store), so any server can handle any request.

mcqs.q: Horizontal scaling means:
options: Adding more machines to share the load
mcqs.explain: Scaling out adds machines; scaling up (vertical) enlarges a single machine.

mcqs.q: A drawback of vertical scaling is:
options: A hardware ceiling and a single point of failure
mcqs.explain: One machine can only get so big, and if it fails the whole service is down.

mcqs.q: Horizontal scaling is easiest when servers are:
options: Stateless (shared state in an external store)
mcqs.explain: Stateless servers let any instance serve any request, so adding machines is straightforward.

u:core-oop-45-database-replication-and-s.title: Database replication and sharding
u:core-oop-45-database-replication-and-s.summary: Copy data for reads/availability vs split data for write scale — two different goals.

blocks.text: Two distinct techniques to scale a database, often confused.

items: **Replication** — keep **copies** of the same data on multiple nodes. A **primary** takes writes; **replicas** serve reads (read scaling) and provide **failover** (availability). Replicas can lag → eventual consistency on reads.
**Sharding (partitioning)** — **split** the data across nodes by a shard key (e.g. user_id range or hash), so each node holds a subset. This scales **writes** and storage since load is divided.

blocks.text: Replication = same data copied (scales reads + availability); sharding = different data split (scales writes + storage). Big systems use both: shard the data, and replicate each shard.
Choosing the shard key is critical — a bad key creates **hotspots** (one shard overloaded). Cross-shard queries and transactions are hard, which is a key trade-off to mention.

mcqs.q: Replication primarily scales:
options: Reads and improves availability (copies of the same data)
mcqs.explain: Replicas serve reads and provide failover; writes still funnel to the primary.

mcqs.q: Sharding primarily helps with:
options: Scaling writes and storage by splitting data across nodes
mcqs.explain: Each shard holds a subset of data, distributing write and storage load.

mcqs.q: A poorly chosen shard key can cause:
options: Hotspots where one shard is overloaded
mcqs.explain: If the key concentrates activity on one shard, that shard becomes a bottleneck (hotspot).

u:core-oop-46-message-queues.title: Message queues
u:core-oop-46-message-queues.summary: Decouple producers from consumers with an async buffer for reliability and load smoothing.

blocks.text: A **message queue** (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS) lets a **producer** send messages that a **consumer** processes later, asynchronously. It decouples the two so they can scale and fail independently.

items: **Decoupling** — the producer doesn't wait for or even know the consumer.
**Load smoothing / buffering** — a traffic spike queues up instead of overwhelming the consumer.
**Reliability** — messages persist until acknowledged, surviving consumer crashes.
**Async work** — offload slow tasks (emails, image processing) from the request path.

blocks.text: Queues turn synchronous coupling into asynchronous, resilient flow: producers and consumers scale separately, spikes are absorbed, and work isn't lost if a consumer restarts. This is the backbone of event-driven architectures.
Delivery guarantees: at-most-once, at-least-once (may duplicate — make consumers idempotent), exactly-once (hardest). Mention idempotency for at-least-once systems.

mcqs.q: A message queue primarily provides:
options: Asynchronous decoupling of producers and consumers with buffering and reliability
mcqs.explain: It lets producers and consumers work independently, smoothing load and persisting messages until processed.

mcqs.q: During a traffic spike, a queue helps by:
options: Buffering messages so consumers process them at their own pace
mcqs.explain: The queue absorbs the burst, letting consumers drain it steadily instead of being overwhelmed.

mcqs.q: With at-least-once delivery, consumers should be:
options: Idempotent, so duplicate messages don't cause harm
mcqs.explain: At-least-once can deliver duplicates, so processing must be idempotent to stay correct.

u:core-oop-47-cdn.title: CDN
u:core-oop-47-cdn.summary: Serve static content from edge servers near users to cut latency and origin load.

blocks.text: A **Content Delivery Network** is a globally distributed network of **edge servers** that cache static content (images, video, CSS/JS) close to users, so requests are served from a nearby location instead of the far-away origin.

items: **Lower latency** — content travels a shorter distance to the user.
**Less origin load** — the CDN absorbs most requests, protecting the origin.
**Availability & DDoS absorption** — the distributed edge soaks up traffic spikes.
Uses TTLs and cache invalidation; best for static/cacheable content.

blocks.text: A CDN is geographic caching: put content at the edge, near users. It's the standard answer for delivering static assets and video at scale with low latency and origin protection.
Dynamic, user-specific content is harder to cache at the edge; CDNs cache it via short TTLs or edge computing, but static assets are the primary win.

mcqs.q: A CDN reduces latency by:
options: Serving cached content from edge servers geographically near the user
mcqs.explain: Edge caching shortens the distance data travels, cutting latency.

mcqs.q: CDNs are most effective for:
options: Static, cacheable content like images, video, CSS/JS
mcqs.explain: Static assets cache well at the edge; highly dynamic per-user data is harder to cache.

mcqs.q: Besides latency, a CDN also:
options: Reduces origin load and helps absorb traffic spikes/DDoS
mcqs.explain: By serving most requests from the edge, it offloads the origin and cushions spikes.

u:core-oop-48-consistent-hashing.title: Consistent hashing
u:core-oop-48-consistent-hashing.summary: Distribute keys across nodes so adding/removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys.

blocks.text: With plain `hash(key) % N` sharding, changing the number of nodes N remaps **almost every key** — catastrophic for a cache/DB. **Consistent hashing** solves this.
How it works

items: Map both **nodes** and **keys** onto a circular hash ring (0 … 2^32-1).
A key belongs to the **first node clockwise** from its position.
Add/remove a node and only the keys between it and its predecessor move — about **1/N** of keys, not all.
**Virtual nodes** (each physical node placed at many ring points) even out the distribution and smooth load on failure.

blocks.text: The win: scaling the cluster remaps only ~K/N keys instead of nearly all. This is why distributed caches (Memcached clients), DynamoDB, and Cassandra use consistent hashing — nodes can join/leave with minimal reshuffling.
Virtual nodes fix uneven distribution and hotspots by giving each server many small arcs on the ring instead of one big one.

mcqs.q: The main advantage of consistent hashing over hash % N is that adding/removing a node:
options: Remaps only about 1/N of the keys
mcqs.explain: Only keys near the changed node move, roughly K/N, versus remapping nearly everything with modulo hashing.

mcqs.q: In consistent hashing, a key is assigned to:
options: The first node clockwise from the key's position on the ring
The node with the lowest id
mcqs.explain: Keys map to the next node clockwise on the hash ring.

mcqs.q: Virtual nodes are used to:
options: Even out key distribution and avoid hotspots
mcqs.explain: Placing each physical node at many ring positions balances load and smooths redistribution when nodes change.

u:core-oop-49-designing-a-url-shortener-.title: Designing a URL shortener end to end
u:core-oop-49-designing-a-url-shortener-.summary: Put the pieces together: API, unique-id generation, storage, caching, and scale.

blocks.text: A full URL-shortener design combines the LLD (code generation) with HLD (scale). Walk it top-down.
Requirements & scale

items: Functional: shorten a URL, redirect on the short code, optional custom alias/expiry/analytics.
Scale: read-heavy (redirects >> creates), so optimise reads. Estimate QPS and storage (back-of-envelope).

blocks.text: Design

items: **API**: `POST /shorten`, `GET /{code}` (302 redirect).
**Unique code**: base62 of a globally unique id — from a distributed counter / **id generator** (e.g. a range-allocating service or Snowflake-style id), avoiding collision checks.
**Storage**: a KV store (code → longUrl), which shards cleanly by code.
**Cache**: hot codes in Redis in front of the store — redirects are read-heavy and highly cacheable.
**Scale-out**: stateless app servers behind a load balancer; shard the KV store; a CDN/edge can cache popular redirects.

blocks.text: The two decisions that carry the interview: (1) generate unique short codes without collisions (base62 of a unique id, not a hash), and (2) make reads fast and scalable (cache + KV store + statelessness), because redirects vastly outnumber creates.
Use a 302 (temporary) redirect if you want to count clicks (each hit reaches your server); a 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers and skips your analytics.

mcqs.q: A URL shortener's workload is characterised as:
mcqs.explain: Redirects (reads) vastly exceed shortening (writes), so the design optimises fast, cacheable reads.

mcqs.q: To generate collision-free short codes at scale, use:
options: Base62 of a globally unique id (e.g. from a distributed id generator)
mcqs.explain: Encoding a unique id guarantees no collisions without extra checks, unlike random/hash approaches.

mcqs.q: Using a 302 (temporary) redirect instead of 301 (permanent) lets you:
options: Count each click, since requests still reach your server
mcqs.explain: 301s are cached by browsers and bypass your server on repeat hits; 302s reach your server so clicks can be tracked.

u:core-oop-20-single-responsibility-viol.title: Single Responsibility Principle
u:core-oop-20-single-responsibility-viol.summary: A class should have exactly one reason to change — one job.

blocks.text: The **S** in SOLID: a class should have **one responsibility**, i.e. one reason to change. If a class does report generation *and* database access *and* email sending, three unrelated forces can force it to change.
Violation and fix

A `Report` class that formats data, saves to a file, and emails it violates SRP. Split it: a `Report` (data), a `ReportFormatter`, a `ReportRepository` (persistence), and a `Mailer`. Each now changes for one reason only.
SRP is about **reasons to change**, not 'do one thing'. Group code that changes together for the same reason; separate code that changes for different reasons. This limits the blast radius of edits.
A telltale sign of an SRP violation: the word 'and' when describing what a class does ('parses AND validates AND stores').

mcqs.q: The Single Responsibility Principle states a class should have:
mcqs.explain: SRP is about a single reason to change — a single responsibility/axis of change.

mcqs.q: A class that formats, persists, and emails a report violates SRP because:
options: It has multiple unrelated reasons to change
mcqs.explain: Formatting, persistence, and mailing are three independent concerns, each a separate reason to change.

mcqs.q: Following SRP typically improves:
options: Maintainability by localising changes to one responsibility per class
mcqs.explain: Separating concerns limits how far a change ripples, making the code easier to maintain and test.

u:core-oop-21-open-closed-violation-and-.title: Open/Closed Principle
u:core-oop-21-open-closed-violation-and-.summary: Open for extension, closed for modification — add behaviour without editing tested code.

blocks.text: The **O** in SOLID: software entities should be **open for extension but closed for modification**. You should be able to add new behaviour without changing existing, working code.
Violation and fix

A `switch(shape.type)` computing area, with a new `case` added for every new shape, violates OCP — every new shape edits the same method. Fix: an abstract `Shape` with an `area()` method that each subclass implements. Adding a `Triangle` means adding a class, not editing the calculator.

OCP is achieved through **abstraction and polymorphism**: depend on an interface, and add new implementations rather than editing a growing conditional. New requirements → new code, not modified code.
A long `if/else` or `switch` on a type code is the classic OCP smell — every new variant reopens that method and risks breaking the others.

mcqs.q: The Open/Closed Principle says software should be:
options: Open for modification, closed for extension
Open for extension, closed for modification
mcqs.explain: You should add new behaviour by extension (new classes) without modifying existing tested code.

mcqs.q: A growing switch statement on a type code violates OCP because:
options: Each new type forces editing the same existing method
mcqs.explain: Adding a variant reopens and risks breaking the shared method — the opposite of closed-for-modification.

mcqs.q: OCP is typically achieved via:
mcqs.explain: Depending on an abstraction lets you plug in new implementations without touching existing code.

u:core-oop-22-liskov-substitution-violat.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
u:core-oop-22-liskov-substitution-violat.summary: A subclass must be usable anywhere its base is expected, without surprising behaviour.

blocks.text: The **L** in SOLID: objects of a subclass should be **substitutable** for their base class without breaking correctness. A subtype must honour the base type's contract.
The classic violation

`Square extends Rectangle` seems fine, but if `setWidth` also changes height (to stay square), code that expects `setWidth` to change only width breaks. `Square` isn't a behavioural subtype of `Rectangle`, so it violates LSP even though a square 'is a' rectangle mathematically.
LSP is about **behavioural** substitutability, not just is-a. A subclass must not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or throw unexpected exceptions where the base wouldn't.
Another red flag: a subclass overriding a method to throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g. an immutable list's `add`) — it breaks callers relying on the base contract.

mcqs.q: The Liskov Substitution Principle requires that:
options: Subtype objects can replace base-type objects without breaking correctness
mcqs.explain: Anywhere the base type is expected, a subtype must work correctly, honouring the base's contract.

mcqs.q: Square extending Rectangle can violate LSP because:
options: Setting width also changing height breaks code expecting independent width/height
mcqs.explain: The Square's coupled setters break the behavioural contract callers rely on for a Rectangle.

mcqs.q: A subclass overriding a method to throw UnsupportedOperationException:
options: Violates LSP by not honouring the base contract
mcqs.explain: Callers expect the base behaviour; throwing where the base wouldn't breaks substitutability.

u:core-oop-23-interface-segregation-viol.title: Interface Segregation Principle
u:core-oop-23-interface-segregation-viol.summary: Prefer many small, focused interfaces over one fat interface clients are forced to implement.

blocks.text: The **I** in SOLID: clients should not be forced to depend on methods they don't use. Split a large 'fat' interface into smaller, role-specific ones.
Violation and fix

A `Machine` interface with `print()`, `scan()`, `fax()` forces a simple printer to implement `scan` and `fax` with empty or throwing bodies. Fix: separate `Printer`, `Scanner`, `Fax` interfaces; a multifunction device implements all three, a basic printer just `Printer`.
ISP prevents 'interface pollution': no class should be forced to implement irrelevant methods. Small, cohesive interfaces keep implementations honest and reduce coupling.
Empty method bodies or ones that throw 'not supported' are the classic sign a fat interface needs segregating.

mcqs.q: The Interface Segregation Principle recommends:
options: Many small, client-specific interfaces instead of a fat one
mcqs.explain: Clients should depend only on the methods they actually use, favouring small focused interfaces.

mcqs.q: A printer forced to implement scan() and fax() with empty bodies indicates:
mcqs.explain: Being forced to implement unused methods signals the interface is too broad and should be split.

mcqs.q: Segregating interfaces reduces:
options: Coupling and forced dependencies on unused methods
The number of classes to zero
mcqs.explain: Focused interfaces mean classes depend only on what they use, lowering coupling.

u:core-oop-24-dependency-inversion-viola.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
u:core-oop-24-dependency-inversion-viola.summary: Depend on abstractions, not concretions — high-level policy shouldn't hinge on low-level details.

blocks.text: The **D** in SOLID: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on **abstractions**. And abstractions shouldn't depend on details — details depend on abstractions.
Violation and fix

An `OrderService` that directly creates a `MySQLDatabase` is welded to that concrete class. Fix: define a `Repository` interface; `OrderService` depends on `Repository`, and a `MySQLRepository` implements it — injected in via the constructor. Now you can swap the database or use a fake in tests.

DIP + dependency injection decouple policy from implementation: the high-level class asks for an interface and is handed a concrete implementation from outside. This is the backbone of testable, flexible systems.
'Inversion' means the direction of dependency is flipped: instead of high-level code depending on low-level code, both depend on an abstraction owned by the high-level side.

mcqs.q: The Dependency Inversion Principle says modules should depend on:
mcqs.explain: Both high- and low-level modules depend on abstractions, decoupling policy from implementation.

mcqs.q: Injecting a Repository interface into OrderService instead of newing a MySQLDatabase:
options: Follows DIP and enables swapping implementations and testing
mcqs.explain: Depending on the interface (and injecting the concrete) decouples the service from the database, aiding testing.

mcqs.q: Dependency injection is commonly used to:
options: Supply a class's dependencies from outside, supporting DIP
mcqs.explain: DI provides the concrete implementation of an abstraction externally, realising dependency inversion.

u:core-oop-25-singleton-and-why-it-is-of.title: Singleton (and why it is often a smell)
u:core-oop-25-singleton-and-why-it-is-of.summary: Guarantee a single shared instance — useful, but easy to abuse as hidden global state.

blocks.text: The **Singleton** pattern ensures a class has only **one instance** and provides a global access point to it (e.g. a config manager, a logger).

items: Private constructor + a static `getInstance()` that lazily creates and returns the sole instance.
In multithreaded code it must be made **thread-safe** (double-checked locking, or an eager static / enum in Java).
It's a **creational** pattern.

blocks.text: Why it's often a smell: a Singleton is global mutable state in disguise. It hides dependencies (code can grab it anywhere), makes unit testing hard (can't easily substitute a fake), and can create hidden coupling. Prefer dependency injection of a single instance.
In Java the cleanest thread-safe singleton is a single-element enum; it also handles serialization correctly.

mcqs.q: The Singleton pattern guarantees:
options: Exactly one instance with a global access point
mcqs.explain: Singleton restricts a class to a single instance accessible globally.

mcqs.q: A common criticism of Singleton is that it:
options: Introduces hidden global mutable state, hurting testability
mcqs.explain: It acts as global state, hides dependencies, and makes substituting test doubles difficult.

mcqs.q: Making a lazily-initialised Singleton safe under concurrency requires:
options: Thread-safety (e.g. double-checked locking or an eager/enum singleton)
mcqs.explain: Without synchronization, two threads could create two instances; thread-safe initialization is needed.

u:core-oop-26-factory-and-abstract-facto.title: Factory and Abstract Factory
u:core-oop-26-factory-and-abstract-facto.summary: Centralise object creation behind a method or a family-producing interface.

blocks.text: Both are **creational** patterns that move object creation out of client code.

items: **Factory Method** — a method decides which concrete subclass to instantiate based on input, returning the base type. The client says `ShapeFactory.create("circle")` and gets a `Shape`.

**Abstract Factory** — an interface that creates **families** of related objects. A `GUIFactory` produces a matching `Button` and `Checkbox`; a `WindowsFactory` and `MacFactory` each produce a consistent set.

blocks.text: Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates a family of related products that must be used together. Both let clients depend on abstractions and honour OCP — add a new type/family without editing client code.
Use a factory when object creation is complex, conditional, or should be decoupled from the client; use Abstract Factory when products come in interchangeable, consistent sets (e.g. per-OS widgets).

mcqs.q: The Factory Method pattern primarily:
options: Encapsulates which concrete class to instantiate, returning a base type
mcqs.explain: It centralises creation, deciding the concrete subtype while the client works with the abstraction.

mcqs.q: Abstract Factory differs from Factory Method by creating:
options: Families of related objects meant to be used together
mcqs.explain: Abstract Factory produces a consistent set of related products (e.g. matching UI widgets per platform).

mcqs.q: Factories help satisfy which principle?
options: Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion (clients depend on abstractions)
mcqs.explain: Clients depend on the product interface and factory abstraction, so new types can be added without editing clients.

u:core-oop-27-builder.title: Builder
u:core-oop-27-builder.summary: Construct a complex object step by step, avoiding telescoping constructors.

blocks.text: The **Builder** pattern (creational) constructs a complex object step by step, so you don't need a constructor with many (often optional) parameters — the 'telescoping constructor' problem.

Pizza p = new Pizza.Builder()
    .size(12)
    .cheese(true)
    .topping("olives")
    .build();

items: Readable, fluent construction; each step is named, so no guessing which boolean is which.
Supports optional parameters cleanly and can enforce validity in `build()`.
Can produce immutable objects (fields set once at build).

blocks.text: Use Builder when a class has many parameters, several optional, or complex construction rules. It replaces confusing multi-argument constructors with readable, self-documenting chained calls.

mcqs.q: The Builder pattern solves the problem of:
options: Constructors with many (often optional) parameters — telescoping constructors
mcqs.explain: Builder assembles an object via readable steps, avoiding unwieldy multi-argument constructors.

mcqs.q: A benefit of Builder is:
options: Readable, fluent, self-documenting construction and easy optional parameters
mcqs.explain: Named chained steps make construction clear, handle optionals well, and can validate in build().

mcqs.q: Builder is categorised as a:
mcqs.explain: Builder is a creational pattern focused on constructing objects.

u:core-oop-28-adapter.title: Adapter
u:core-oop-28-adapter.summary: Wrap an incompatible interface so an existing class can be used where another interface is expected.

blocks.text: The **Adapter** pattern (structural) converts one interface into another that a client expects, letting classes with incompatible interfaces work together — like a physical power-plug adapter.

items: A client expects interface `Target`; you have a class with a different interface `Adaptee`. The `Adapter` implements `Target` and internally calls `Adaptee`.
Common when integrating a third-party or legacy class you can't change.

blocks.text: Adapter reconciles interfaces. It doesn't add behaviour (that's Decorator) — it translates calls so an existing class fits where a different interface is required.
Distinguish: Adapter changes an interface; Decorator adds responsibilities keeping the same interface; Facade simplifies a whole subsystem behind one interface.

mcqs.q: The Adapter pattern is used to:
options: Add new behaviour to an object
Convert one interface into another a client expects
mcqs.explain: Adapter translates an existing (incompatible) interface into the one the client needs.

mcqs.q: Adapter differs from Decorator in that Adapter:
options: Changes/translates the interface rather than adding behaviour
mcqs.explain: Adapter reconciles interfaces; Decorator adds responsibilities while preserving the interface.

mcqs.q: A typical use of Adapter is:
options: Integrating a legacy or third-party class with an incompatible interface
mcqs.explain: It wraps a class you can't modify so it conforms to the required interface.

u:core-oop-29-decorator.title: Decorator
u:core-oop-29-decorator.summary: Attach responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it, keeping the same interface.

blocks.text: The **Decorator** pattern (structural) adds behaviour to an object at runtime by **wrapping** it in another object with the **same interface**. Wrappers can be stacked.

Coffee c = new Milk(new Sugar(new Espresso()));
c.cost();   // espresso + sugar + milk

items: Each decorator implements the component interface and holds a reference to a wrapped component, adding to its behaviour before/after delegating.
A flexible alternative to subclassing for every combination (Espresso+Milk, Espresso+Sugar, Espresso+Milk+Sugar…).

blocks.text: Decorator adds responsibilities dynamically and composably, avoiding a subclass explosion. The wrappers share the base interface, so a decorated object is still usable everywhere the plain one is (the java.io streams are the textbook example).

mcqs.q: The Decorator pattern adds behaviour by:
options: Wrapping an object in another with the same interface
Creating a subclass for each feature
mcqs.explain: Decorators wrap a component, sharing its interface and augmenting behaviour, and can be stacked.

mcqs.q: Decorator is preferred over subclassing when:
options: Many combinations of features would cause a subclass explosion
You want to change the interface
mcqs.explain: Composable wrappers handle feature combinations without a class per combination.

mcqs.q: A decorated object can be used wherever the base component is because:
options: It implements the same interface as the component
mcqs.explain: Sharing the component interface keeps decorated objects substitutable for undecorated ones.

u:core-oop-30-observer.title: Observer
u:core-oop-30-observer.summary: Notify a set of dependents automatically when a subject's state changes.

blocks.text: The **Observer** pattern (behavioural) defines a one-to-many dependency: when a **subject** changes state, all registered **observers** are notified automatically. It's the basis of event systems and MVC.

items: Observers `subscribe`/`register` with the subject; the subject calls `notify()` on each when its state changes.
Decouples the subject from its observers — the subject knows only the observer interface, not concrete listeners.
Powers UI event listeners, pub-sub, reactive streams, and model→view updates.

blocks.text: Observer decouples 'something changed' from 'who reacts'. The subject broadcasts to an abstract observer interface, so listeners can be added/removed without the subject knowing their concrete types.
Watch for memory leaks: observers that forget to unsubscribe keep the subject referencing them. And beware notification storms / ordering assumptions.

mcqs.q: The Observer pattern establishes:
options: A one-to-many notification from a subject to its observers
mcqs.explain: When the subject's state changes, all subscribed observers are notified — a one-to-many dependency.

mcqs.q: Observer decouples the subject from observers because the subject:
options: Depends only on an observer interface, not concrete listeners
mcqs.explain: The subject notifies through an abstract interface, so concrete observers can vary independently.

mcqs.q: A common real-world use of Observer is:
options: UI event listeners / pub-sub / model-view updates
mcqs.explain: Event listeners and MVC view updates are canonical Observer applications.

u:core-oop-31-strategy.title: Strategy
u:core-oop-31-strategy.summary: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and swap them at runtime.

blocks.text: The **Strategy** pattern (behavioural) defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each behind a common interface, and makes them interchangeable at runtime. The context delegates the varying behaviour to a strategy object.

sorter.setStrategy(new QuickSort());
sorter.sort(data);          // swap to new MergeSort() anytime

items: Replaces a big conditional selecting behaviour with a set of strategy classes.
The context holds a reference to a `Strategy` interface and calls it, unaware of the concrete algorithm.
Favours **composition over inheritance** — behaviour is injected, not baked into a subclass.

blocks.text: Strategy makes an algorithm a plug-in: the context depends on the strategy interface, so you swap or add algorithms without touching the context. It's the OCP-friendly alternative to a behaviour-selecting switch.

mcqs.q: The Strategy pattern lets you:
options: Select and swap interchangeable algorithms at runtime behind a common interface
mcqs.explain: Encapsulated algorithms behind one interface can be chosen/replaced at runtime by the context.

mcqs.q: Strategy typically replaces:
options: A large conditional that selects behaviour, with pluggable strategy classes
mcqs.explain: Instead of branching to pick behaviour, each behaviour becomes a strategy the context delegates to.

mcqs.q: Strategy embodies which design guidance?
mcqs.explain: Behaviour is composed in via a strategy object rather than fixed by subclassing.

u:core-oop-32-command.title: Command
u:core-oop-32-command.summary: Wrap a request as an object, enabling queueing, logging, and undo.

blocks.text: The **Command** pattern (behavioural) encapsulates a request as an object with an `execute()` method, decoupling the **invoker** (what triggers it) from the **receiver** (what performs it).

items: Each command holds everything needed to perform an action; the invoker just calls `execute()`.
Because a request is now an object, you can **queue** commands, **log** them, and support **undo** (add `undo()`).
Used in menu/button actions, task queues, transactional systems, and macro recording.

blocks.text: Turning a request into an object is what unlocks undo/redo, queuing, and logging — you can store, pass, and reverse actions. The invoker is decoupled from how the action is carried out.
Undo is implemented by having each command remember enough state to reverse itself in undo(); a stack of executed commands gives multi-level undo.

mcqs.q: The Command pattern encapsulates:
options: A request as an object with an execute() method
mcqs.explain: A request becomes an object, decoupling the invoker from the receiver that performs it.

mcqs.q: Representing requests as command objects enables:
options: Queueing, logging, and undo/redo of actions
mcqs.explain: As first-class objects, commands can be stored, replayed, logged, and reversed.

mcqs.q: Undo in the Command pattern is typically supported by:
options: An undo() method that reverses the command's effect
mcqs.explain: Each command remembers how to reverse itself via undo(), often tracked on a stack for multi-level undo.

u:core-oop-33-composition-over-inheritan.title: Composition over inheritance
u:core-oop-33-composition-over-inheritan.summary: Prefer assembling behaviour from parts (has-a) over deep class hierarchies (is-a).

blocks.text: **Composition over inheritance** is the guideline to build behaviour by **composing** objects (has-a) rather than inheriting from a base class (is-a), unless there's a genuine is-a relationship.

items: Inheritance is **rigid**: it's fixed at compile time, exposes the base's internals to subclasses (fragile base class), and deep hierarchies are hard to change.
Composition is **flexible**: behaviour is assembled from parts and can be swapped at runtime (Strategy is composition in action).
A `Car` should **have** an `Engine` (composition), not **be** an `Engine`.

blocks.text: Use inheritance only for true is-a relationships that share behaviour and satisfy LSP. For reuse and flexibility, compose: delegate to member objects. This is the single most repeated piece of OOP design advice.
The 'fragile base class problem': changes to a base class can silently break subclasses that depend on its internals — a cost composition avoids.

mcqs.q: Composition over inheritance advises building behaviour primarily via:
options: Has-a relationships (composing objects) rather than is-a inheritance
mcqs.explain: Assembling behaviour from member objects is more flexible than inheriting it.

mcqs.q: A key drawback of inheritance that composition avoids is:
options: Rigidity and the fragile base class problem (subclasses coupled to base internals)
mcqs.explain: Inheritance couples subclasses to base internals and is fixed at compile time; composition is looser and swappable.

mcqs.q: Inheritance is appropriate when:
options: There is a genuine is-a relationship that satisfies Liskov substitution
mcqs.explain: Reserve inheritance for true is-a subtypes that honour the base contract; otherwise compose.

u:core-oop-0-encapsulation-with-code-not.title: Encapsulation
u:core-oop-0-encapsulation-with-code-not.summary: Bundle data with the methods that guard it, and expose only a controlled interface.

blocks.text: **Encapsulation** means keeping an object's data (**fields**) private and exposing it only through methods that enforce the object's rules. The outside world can't put the object into an invalid state because it never touches the fields directly.

items: The `private` field + validating methods mean `balance` can never go negative through a bad deposit.
It is NOT just 'making fields private' — the point is protecting **invariants** behind a controlled interface.
Enables changing the internal representation later without breaking callers (they only depend on the methods).

blocks.text: Encapsulation = data + behaviour bundled, with access controlled to protect invariants. Abstraction is about *what* is exposed; encapsulation is about *hiding the internals* that back it.

mcqs.q: The primary purpose of encapsulation is to:
options: Protect an object's invariants by controlling access to its internal state
mcqs.explain: By hiding fields and exposing validating methods, an object can't be pushed into an invalid state from outside.

mcqs.q: Encapsulation makes future changes safer because:
options: Callers depend only on the public interface, so internals can change without breaking them
It removes the need for tests
mcqs.explain: As long as the public methods keep their contract, the internal representation can be changed freely.

mcqs.q: Which best distinguishes encapsulation from abstraction?
options: Encapsulation hides internal state/implementation; abstraction exposes only the essential concept
Abstraction hides data; encapsulation shows it
mcqs.explain: Abstraction is about the simplified external view; encapsulation is the mechanism of hiding internals behind it.

u:core-oop-1-abstraction.title: Abstraction
u:core-oop-1-abstraction.summary: Expose only the essential behaviour and hide the messy how — model the idea, not the details.

blocks.text: **Abstraction** means representing a concept by its essential behaviour while hiding the implementation. A `List` interface says you can `add` and `get`; whether it's backed by an array or linked nodes is hidden.

items: Achieved with **abstract classes** and **interfaces**: they declare *what* an object does, not *how*.
Reduces complexity — callers reason about a small contract instead of internals.
Lets multiple implementations be swapped behind the same interface (polymorphism).

blocks.text: Abstraction manages complexity by hiding detail behind a simple contract; encapsulation is the enforcement mechanism that keeps that detail hidden. They work together.
Driving analogy: the steering wheel and pedals are the abstraction; you don't need to know the engine's internals to drive. That interface is stable even if the engine changes.

mcqs.q: Abstraction primarily helps by:
options: Hiding implementation detail behind a simple, essential interface to manage complexity
mcqs.explain: It exposes only what matters (the contract) and hides how it's done, reducing the complexity callers must handle.

mcqs.q: In Java/C++, abstraction is commonly expressed with:
mcqs.explain: Interfaces and abstract classes declare behaviour (the what) without dictating implementation (the how).

mcqs.q: A benefit of programming to an abstraction (interface) is:
options: You must know every implementation detail
Implementations can be swapped without changing calling code
mcqs.explain: Callers depend on the contract, so any conforming implementation can be substituted — the basis of polymorphism and testability.

u:core-oop-2-inheritance-and-its-types.title: Inheritance and its types
u:core-oop-2-inheritance-and-its-types.summary: Derive a class from another to reuse and specialise — single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid.

blocks.text: **Inheritance** lets a class (child/derived) acquire the fields and methods of another (parent/base), modelling an **is-a** relationship (a `Dog` is-an `Animal`). It enables reuse and lets the child extend or override behaviour.

rows: B and C both inherit A
C inherits A and B (C++ yes; Java only via interfaces)

blocks.text: Java forbids multiple inheritance of classes to avoid the **diamond problem** (ambiguity when two parents provide the same member); it allows multiple interface inheritance instead. C++ allows it but needs virtual inheritance to resolve the diamond.
Favour inheritance only for genuine is-a relationships. For 'has-a' or 'can-do', prefer composition — over-using inheritance creates fragile, tightly-coupled hierarchies.

mcqs.q: Inheritance models which relationship?
mcqs.explain: A derived class is-a specialised version of its base class (a Dog is-an Animal).

mcqs.q: Java disallows multiple inheritance of classes primarily to avoid:
mcqs.explain: Two base classes providing the same member create ambiguity (the diamond problem); Java sidesteps it by allowing only interface multiple inheritance.

mcqs.q: 'C inherits B, which inherits A' is which type of inheritance?
mcqs.explain: A chain of derivations (A→B→C) is multilevel inheritance.

u:core-oop-3-polymorphism-compile-time-v.title: Polymorphism: compile-time vs runtime
u:core-oop-3-polymorphism-compile-time-v.summary: One interface, many forms — resolved either at compile time (overloading) or at runtime (overriding).

blocks.text: **Polymorphism** lets the same call behave differently depending on context. There are two kinds, distinguished by **when the actual method is chosen**.

rows: At runtime by the object's actual type

blocks.text:
Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();   // runtime: Dog.speak() runs, not Animal.speak()

Runtime polymorphism is the powerful one: a base-type reference invokes the derived object's overridden method via **dynamic dispatch** (the vtable in C++). This is what lets you write code against the base type and plug in any subclass.
Overloading (same method name, different parameter lists) is resolved at compile time and is NOT true runtime polymorphism — a common trick question.

mcqs.q: Method overriding provides which kind of polymorphism?
mcqs.explain: Overriding is resolved at runtime based on the object's actual type — dynamic/runtime polymorphism.

mcqs.q: Method overloading is resolved:
options: At compile time by the method signature
mcqs.explain: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types/signature — compile-time (static) polymorphism.

mcqs.q: For `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` to call Dog's speak(), speak() must be:
mcqs.explain: Dynamic dispatch requires the method be virtual/overridable so the runtime picks the subclass version.

u:core-oop-4-abstract-class-vs-interface.title: Abstract class vs interface: when each
u:core-oop-4-abstract-class-vs-interface.summary: Share partial implementation and state, or define a pure capability contract.

blocks.text: Both let you program to an abstraction, but they serve different design intents.

Use an **abstract class** when subclasses share common state/behaviour (an is-a with reusable code). Use an **interface** to declare a capability many unrelated classes can implement (Comparable, Serializable). Prefer interfaces for flexibility.
A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one abstract class — so interfaces are the way to give a class multiple, orthogonal capabilities.

mcqs.q: Which can hold instance fields (state)?
mcqs.explain: Abstract classes can have instance fields and constructors; interfaces hold only constants (plus default/static methods in modern Java).

mcqs.q: You want many unrelated classes to share a capability like 'Comparable'. Use:
options: An abstract base class they all extend
mcqs.explain: Unrelated classes can each implement the interface without forcing a common base class — that's the interface's role.

mcqs.q: A key structural limit is that a class can:
options: Implement many interfaces but extend only one class
mcqs.explain: Single class inheritance but multiple interface implementation is why interfaces model orthogonal capabilities.

u:core-oop-5-constructors-default-parame.title: Constructors: default, parameterised, copy
u:core-oop-5-constructors-default-parame.summary: Special functions that initialise an object; the compiler supplies some for free.

blocks.text: A **constructor** initialises a new object; it has the class's name and no return type. Three common forms:

items: **Default** — no parameters; sets fields to defaults. The compiler generates one **only if you declare no constructors**.
**Parameterised** — takes arguments to initialise fields to given values.
**Copy** — creates a new object as a copy of an existing one (`Foo(const Foo& other)` in C++).

blocks.text: The moment you declare any constructor (e.g. a parameterised one), the compiler stops generating the default constructor. If you still need a no-arg one, you must declare it explicitly.
In C++ the compiler also auto-generates a copy constructor that does a member-wise (shallow) copy — which is a bug for classes owning raw pointers. See the copy-constructor and rule-of-three notes.

mcqs.q: When does the compiler NOT provide a default constructor?
options: When you have declared any other constructor
When the class has no fields
mcqs.explain: Declaring any constructor suppresses the implicit default; you must add a no-arg constructor yourself if needed.

mcqs.q: A copy constructor is used to:
options: Initialise an object from another object of the same type
mcqs.explain: It constructs a new object as a copy of an existing instance.

mcqs.q: A constructor is distinguished from a normal method because it:
options: Has the class's name and no return type
mcqs.explain: Constructors share the class name and declare no return type; they run on object creation.

u:core-oop-6-copy-constructor-vs-assignm.title: Copy constructor vs assignment operator
u:core-oop-6-copy-constructor-vs-assignm.summary: One builds a brand-new object from another; the other overwrites an already-built object.

blocks.text: In C++ these are easily confused because both copy one object into another, but they run at different moments.

rows: A new object is being created from another
An existing object is assigned another
Release old resources, then copy, guard self-assignment

blocks.text: The distinction: the copy constructor builds a new object (no old state to clean up); operator= must first release the target's existing resources and guard against self-assignment (`if (this == &other) return *this;`).
For a class owning a raw pointer, the compiler-generated versions do a shallow copy — two objects end up owning the same pointer, causing a double free. This is why the rule of three exists.

mcqs.q: In `Foo b = a;`, which is invoked?
mcqs.explain: b is a new object, so the copy constructor runs — even though the syntax uses '='.

mcqs.q: What must the copy assignment operator do that the copy constructor need not?
options: Release the target's existing resources and guard self-assignment
Call the destructor of the source
mcqs.explain: The target already holds resources; operator= must free them and handle self-assignment, unlike a fresh construction.

mcqs.q: The compiler-generated copy operations do a:
mcqs.explain: Default copies are member-wise (shallow), which is unsafe for classes managing raw pointers/resources.

u:core-oop-7-destructor-and-virtual-dest.title: Destructor and virtual destructor
u:core-oop-7-destructor-and-virtual-dest.summary: Clean up an object's resources — and why the base destructor must be virtual for polymorphic deletion.

blocks.text: A **destructor** (`~Foo()`) runs when an object is destroyed, releasing resources it owns (memory, files, locks). In C++ it's where you free what the constructor acquired.
Why virtual

If you delete a derived object through a **base-class pointer** and the base destructor is **not virtual**, only the base destructor runs — the derived part leaks. Making the base destructor `virtual` ensures the full chain (derived then base) runs.

Base* p = new Derived();
delete p;   // Only Base::~Base runs unless ~Base is virtual
Rule: any class intended to be used as a base class (deleted polymorphically) must have a **virtual destructor**, or you get resource leaks / undefined behaviour.
Destructors run in reverse order of construction: members and base parts are destroyed after the derived body, base last.

mcqs.q: Why should a base class have a virtual destructor?
options: So deleting a derived object via a base pointer runs the full destructor chain
mcqs.explain: Without a virtual destructor, `delete basePtr` on a derived object skips the derived destructor, leaking its resources.

mcqs.q: A destructor's job is to:
options: Release resources the object owns before it is destroyed
mcqs.explain: It performs cleanup (freeing memory, closing files) as the object's lifetime ends.

mcqs.q: Destructors of members and base classes run:
mcqs.explain: Destruction is the reverse of construction: derived body first, then members, then base.

u:core-oop-8-rule-of-three-five.title: Rule of three / five
u:core-oop-8-rule-of-three-five.summary: If you manage a resource, define the copy/move/destroy set together — or none of them.

blocks.text: The **Rule of Three** (C++): if a class needs a custom **destructor**, **copy constructor**, or **copy assignment operator**, it almost certainly needs all three — because it manages a resource whose default shallow copy would be wrong.
The **Rule of Five** adds the two **move** operations (move constructor and move assignment) introduced in C++11, for efficient transfer of resources without copying.

items: Need a destructor to free a resource → the default copy would create two owners of it → you must define copy operations too.
Rule of Five: also define move constructor and move assignment to enable cheap moves.
The **Rule of Zero**: better still, use RAII types (smart pointers, std::string, std::vector) so you need to write none of them.

blocks.text: The unifying idea: resource ownership must be handled consistently across construction, copy, move, and destruction. Manage it in one place (a member RAII type) and the compiler defaults become correct — the Rule of Zero.

mcqs.q: The Rule of Three says if you define one of these, define all three:
options: Destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment operator
mcqs.explain: Needing a custom destructor/copy-ctor/copy-assignment signals resource management, so all three must be handled together.

mcqs.q: The Rule of Five adds which operations to the Rule of Three?
mcqs.explain: C++11 move semantics add the move constructor and move assignment for efficient resource transfer.

mcqs.q: The Rule of Zero recommends:
options: Using RAII members (e.g. smart pointers) so the compiler defaults are correct and you write none
mcqs.explain: Delegating ownership to RAII types makes the implicitly-generated operations correct, so you needn't write any.

u:core-oop-9-shallow-vs-deep-copy.title: Shallow vs deep copy
u:core-oop-9-shallow-vs-deep-copy.summary: Copy the pointer (shared target) or copy what it points to (independent target).

blocks.text: When an object holds a reference/pointer to other data, copying it has two meanings.

items: **Shallow copy** — copies the pointer value, so both objects share the same underlying data. Cheap, but changes via one affect the other, and destroying one frees data the other still uses (**double free / dangling**).
**Deep copy** — allocates new memory and copies the pointed-to contents, so the two objects are fully independent. Safe, but more expensive.

blocks.text: Default/compiler-generated copies are shallow. For a class that owns heap data or other resources, you need a deep copy (or a clear ownership model via smart pointers) to avoid shared-state bugs.
In Java, `Object.clone()` is shallow by default; nested mutable objects must be copied explicitly for a deep clone. Same principle in every language with references.

mcqs.q: A shallow copy of an object containing a pointer results in:
options: Two independent copies of the pointed-to data
Two objects sharing the same underlying data
mcqs.explain: Shallow copy duplicates the pointer, so both objects reference the same data — mutations and frees affect both.

mcqs.q: Deep copy is preferred when:
options: The object owns heap data that must be independent between copies
You want maximum speed regardless of correctness
mcqs.explain: Owning distinct resources requires deep copy so each object independently manages its own data.

mcqs.q: The danger of an unintended shallow copy of an owning object is:
options: Double free / dangling pointer when one copy is destroyed
mcqs.explain: Both copies share and later free the same memory, causing a double free or use-after-free.

u:core-oop-10-static-members.title: static members
u:core-oop-10-static-members.summary: Data and functions that belong to the class itself, not to any single instance.

blocks.text: A **static member** belongs to the class, not to any object. A **static field** is shared by all instances (one copy total); a **static method** can be called without an instance and can access only static members.

items: Static field: a single shared value — e.g. an instance counter, or a configuration constant.
Static method: no `this`; can't access instance (non-static) members directly.
Useful for factory methods, utility functions, and shared caches/counters.

blocks.text: Static = one per class; instance = one per object. A static method has no `this`, which is exactly why it can't touch instance fields.
Overusing static (global mutable state) hurts testability and thread-safety. Shared static state needs synchronisation and makes code harder to reason about.

mcqs.q: A static field is:
options: Shared across all instances of the class (one copy)
mcqs.explain: There is a single static field per class, shared by every instance.

mcqs.q: A static method cannot:
mcqs.explain: Having no `this`, a static method can't directly reach instance fields/methods.

mcqs.q: A good use of a static field is:
options: A shared counter of how many instances were created
mcqs.explain: A shared counter is class-level state, ideal for a static field.

u:core-oop-11-const-correctness.title: const correctness
u:core-oop-11-const-correctness.summary: Mark what must not change so the compiler enforces it and readers can trust it.

blocks.text: **const correctness** (C++) means using `const` wherever a value shouldn't change: parameters, return values, and member functions that don't modify the object.

items: A **const member function** (`int size() const`) promises not to modify the object; only const methods can be called on a const object.
`const T&` parameters avoid copying while promising not to modify the argument.
It documents intent and lets the compiler catch accidental mutation.

blocks.text: const correctness is compiler-enforced documentation: it guarantees a function won't mutate what it says it won't, enabling safe use with const objects and preventing whole classes of bugs.

mcqs.q: A const member function guarantees it will:
mcqs.explain: A const method promises not to change the object, so it's callable on const instances.

mcqs.q: On a `const` object, you may call:
mcqs.explain: A const object permits only const member functions, which promise not to mutate it.

mcqs.q: Passing a large object as `const T&` instead of `T`:
options: Avoids a copy while promising not to modify it
mcqs.explain: A const reference avoids the copy and guarantees the callee won't modify the argument.

u:core-oop-12-friend-functions.title: friend functions
u:core-oop-12-friend-functions.summary: Grant a specific external function or class access to a class's private members.

blocks.text: A **friend** function or class (C++) is granted access to another class's `private` and `protected` members, even though it isn't a member itself. The class explicitly names its friends.

items: Declared inside the class with the `friend` keyword; the friend is not a member and has no `this`.
Common use: overloading operators like `operator<<` (stream output) that must access internals but can't be members of the left operand (`std::ostream`).
Friendship is not inherited and not mutual unless declared both ways.

blocks.text: Friendship deliberately breaks encapsulation, so use it sparingly and intentionally. It's a controlled exception (the class chooses its friends), not a backdoor for arbitrary code.

mcqs.q: A friend function can:
options: Access the private and protected members of the class that declares it a friend
mcqs.explain: Friendship grants access to non-public members, though the friend is not a member of the class.

mcqs.q: A classic use of a friend function is:
options: Overloading operator<< for output, which needs internals but can't be a member of ostream
mcqs.explain: operator<< takes ostream as the left operand, so it's a non-member friend that accesses the class's internals.

mcqs.q: Friendship in C++ is:
options: Not inherited and not automatically mutual
mcqs.explain: Friendship is explicitly granted, not inherited, and not mutual unless each class declares the other.

u:core-oop-13-this-pointer.title: this pointer
u:core-oop-13-this-pointer.summary: The implicit reference to the object a non-static method is operating on.

blocks.text: `this` is an implicit pointer (C++) / reference (Java) available inside non-static methods, pointing to the object the method was called on.

items: Disambiguates a parameter from a field of the same name: `this.x = x;`.
Enables **method chaining** by returning `*this` (`return *this;`).
Used in the copy assignment operator to guard self-assignment: `if (this == &other) return *this;`.
Static methods have no `this` (they aren't tied to an instance).

blocks.text: `this` identifies 'the current object'. Returning it (`return *this;`) is what lets you write `obj.setA(1).setB(2)` fluent chains.

mcqs.q: `this` refers to:
options: The specific object on which the non-static method was invoked
mcqs.explain: `this` points to the current instance the method is running on.

mcqs.q: Which does NOT have access to `this`?
mcqs.explain: Static methods aren't associated with an instance, so there is no `this`.

mcqs.q: Returning `*this` from a setter enables:
mcqs.explain: Returning the current object allows calls to be chained: obj.a().b().c().

u:core-oop-14-operator-overloading.title: Operator overloading
u:core-oop-14-operator-overloading.summary: Define what built-in operators mean for your own types, for natural syntax.

blocks.text: **Operator overloading** (C++) lets you define operators like `+`, `==`, `[]`, `<<` for your own classes so they read naturally (`a + b` for two `Complex` numbers).

items: Implemented as member functions or non-member (often friend) functions.
Should preserve the operator's intuitive meaning — `+` should combine, `==` should compare equality.
Some operators (like `<<` for streams) must be non-members because the left operand isn't your type.

blocks.text: Overload for clarity, not cleverness. Making `+` do something surprising violates the principle of least astonishment and confuses readers. Java deliberately omits operator overloading (except built-in + for strings) for this reason.

mcqs.q: Operator overloading lets you:
options: Add new operators to the language
Define what existing operators mean for your own types
mcqs.explain: You give existing operators meaning for user-defined types; you cannot invent new operators or change precedence.

mcqs.q: operator<< for stream output is usually a:
options: Non-member (often friend) function, since the left operand is ostream
mcqs.explain: The left operand is std::ostream, not your class, so << must be a non-member function.

mcqs.q: Java's stance on operator overloading is:
options: Not supported for user types (to avoid confusing code)
mcqs.explain: Java omits user-defined operator overloading (only built-in + on Strings), prioritising readability.

u:core-oop-15-templates-and-generic-prog.title: Templates and generic programming
u:core-oop-15-templates-and-generic-prog.summary: Write code once that works for any type, with type safety and no duplication.

blocks.text: **Templates** (C++) / **generics** (Java) let you write a class or function parameterised by a type, so one implementation serves many types with compile-time type safety.

template<typename T>
T maxOf(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

rows: Instantiation — a separate version compiled per type
Type erasure — one version, types checked at compile time then erased

blocks.text: The big difference: C++ generates real code per type (instantiation), so it's fast and works with primitives; Java erases the type parameter at runtime (type erasure), which is why you can't do `new T()` or check `instanceof List<String>`.

mcqs.q: C++ templates work by:
options: Instantiating a separate version of the code for each type used
mcqs.explain: The compiler generates a concrete version per instantiated type, giving speed and primitive support.

mcqs.q: Java generics use type erasure, which means:
options: The generic type information is removed after compile-time checks
Each type gets its own class
mcqs.explain: Java erases generic types after compile-time checking, so runtime has no `T` information.

mcqs.q: A consequence of Java's type erasure is that you cannot:
options: Do `new T()` or check `instanceof List<String>` at runtime
mcqs.explain: Because the type is erased, runtime operations needing the actual type parameter aren't allowed.

u:core-oop-16-virtual-functions-and-the-.title: Virtual functions and the vtable
u:core-oop-16-virtual-functions-and-the-.summary: The mechanism behind runtime polymorphism: a per-class table of function pointers.

blocks.text: A **virtual function** can be overridden by a derived class, and the correct version is chosen at **runtime** based on the object's actual type — this is **dynamic dispatch**. It's implemented with a **vtable**.
How the vtable works

items: Each class with virtual functions has a **vtable**: an array of pointers to its virtual function implementations.
Each object holds a hidden **vptr** pointing to its class's vtable.
A virtual call becomes: follow the object's vptr → look up the function in the vtable → call it. So the object's real type decides which override runs.

blocks.text: The vtable is why `basePtr->speak()` calls the derived override: the lookup goes through the object's own vptr, which points to the derived class's table. This indirection is the (small) cost of runtime polymorphism.
Non-virtual calls are resolved at compile time by the pointer's static type — so forgetting `virtual` means the base version is always called, ignoring overrides.

mcqs.q: The vtable is:
options: A per-object copy of all methods
A per-class table of pointers to its virtual function implementations
mcqs.explain: Each polymorphic class has one vtable of virtual-function pointers; each object holds a vptr to it.

mcqs.q: A virtual call is resolved by:
options: Following the object's vptr to its class vtable at runtime
mcqs.explain: Dynamic dispatch uses the object's vptr → vtable, so the actual object type selects the override.

mcqs.q: If a method is NOT virtual, a call through a base pointer invokes:
options: The base version (resolved by the static type)
mcqs.explain: Non-virtual methods bind at compile time to the pointer's static type, ignoring the actual object's overrides.

u:core-oop-17-diamond-problem-and-virtua.title: Diamond problem and virtual inheritance
u:core-oop-17-diamond-problem-and-virtua.summary: When two base classes share a common ancestor, you can get two copies — virtual inheritance fixes it.

blocks.text: The **diamond problem** arises with multiple inheritance: if B and C both inherit A, and D inherits both B and C, then D ends up with **two copies** of A's members, creating ambiguity — which `A::x` does `D` mean?

A
   / \
  B   C
   \ /
    D    // D has two A subobjects unless A is virtually inherited

items: **Virtual inheritance** (`class B : virtual public A`) makes B and C share a single common A subobject, so D has just one A.
Java avoids the problem entirely by disallowing multiple inheritance of classes (interfaces have no state to duplicate).
