blocks.text: Two shared paths to a common base → duplicate base subobject → ambiguity. Virtual inheritance collapses them into one shared base. It's the reason C++ multiple inheritance needs `virtual`.

mcqs.q: The diamond problem occurs when:
options: A class has too many methods
A class inherits from two classes that share a common base, duplicating the base
Two classes have the same name
mcqs.explain: Sharing a common ancestor through two paths yields two base subobjects and ambiguous access.

mcqs.q: C++ resolves the diamond problem with:
options: Virtual inheritance, making a single shared base subobject
mcqs.explain: Declaring the common base as virtual gives one shared instance of it in the most-derived class.

mcqs.q: Java avoids the diamond problem by:
options: Disallowing multiple inheritance of classes (only interfaces)
mcqs.explain: Interfaces carry no state to duplicate, and classes can extend only one class, so the ambiguity can't arise.

u:core-oop-18-raii-and-smart-pointers.title: RAII and smart pointers
u:core-oop-18-raii-and-smart-pointers.summary: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's scope so cleanup is automatic and exception-safe.

blocks.text: **RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)** is the C++ idiom of wrapping a resource (memory, file, lock) in an object that acquires it in its constructor and releases it in its destructor. When the object goes out of scope, cleanup happens automatically — even if an exception is thrown.
Smart pointers apply RAII to memory

RAII makes cleanup deterministic and exception-safe: the destructor runs on scope exit no matter how you leave. Smart pointers are RAII for heap memory, which is why modern C++ rarely uses raw new/delete.
Two shared_ptrs referencing each other form a cycle that never reaches refcount 0 — a leak. Break it with a weak_ptr on one side.

mcqs.q: RAII ties a resource's lifetime to:
options: An object's scope — released in its destructor
mcqs.explain: The resource is acquired in the constructor and released in the destructor, so scope exit guarantees cleanup.

mcqs.q: Which smart pointer models sole ownership?
mcqs.explain: unique_ptr is the non-copyable, movable single-owner pointer — the default for owning heap memory.

mcqs.q: weak_ptr is used to:
options: Observe a shared_ptr without owning it, breaking reference cycles
mcqs.explain: weak_ptr is a non-owning reference that doesn't affect the count, used to break shared_ptr cycles.

u:core-oop-19-exception-handling.title: Exception handling
u:core-oop-19-exception-handling.summary: Separate error handling from normal flow with try/throw/catch, and clean up safely.

blocks.text: **Exceptions** signal errors by transferring control from the point of failure (`throw`) to a handler (`catch`), unwinding the stack in between. This keeps error handling out of the normal code path.

items: `try` wraps code that might fail; `catch` handles specific exception types; `finally` (Java) always runs for cleanup.
**Stack unwinding**: as the exception propagates, destructors of local objects run — which is why RAII gives exception-safe cleanup in C++.
**Checked vs unchecked** (Java): checked exceptions must be declared/handled; unchecked (RuntimeException) need not be.

blocks.text: Exceptions decouple 'what went wrong' from 'where it's handled'. In C++, combine them with RAII so resources are released during unwinding; in Java, use finally or try-with-resources.
Don't use exceptions for normal control flow, and never let a destructor throw (C++) — an exception during unwinding calls std::terminate.

mcqs.q: During exception propagation, the stack is unwound, which in C++ means:
options: Destructors of local objects run, enabling RAII cleanup
mcqs.explain: Stack unwinding destroys local objects, so RAII wrappers release their resources safely.

mcqs.q: In Java, a checked exception:
options: Must be caught or declared in the method signature
mcqs.explain: Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler to be handled or declared; unchecked ones aren't.

mcqs.q: A recommended practice is to:
options: Use exceptions for ordinary control flow
Reserve exceptions for exceptional error conditions, not normal flow
mcqs.explain: Exceptions are for error conditions; using them for regular branching is slow and unclear.
